AL.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Alabama and police use them. They must serve a specific purpose such as catching impaired drivers; a general roadblock to deter "trouble" was struck down.
AL.inPractice: Alabama courts upheld stopping a driver who pulled into a private driveway to avoid a checkpoint (Smith v. State, 1987), so an obvious dodge can itself lead to a stop.
AL.detail: Avoiding a checkpoint can justify a stop

AK.summary: Alaska does not run sobriety checkpoints. No state law authorizes them, so a DUI stop there generally needs an officer's individual suspicion, such as a traffic violation.
AK.inPractice: IIHS (2020) lists Alaska as having "no state authority," and FindLaw (2025) and AAA (2025) list it among states without checkpoints. Unconfirmed: no Alaska statute, ruling, or agency statement was found.

AZ.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Arizona and police use them regularly. Arizona courts have upheld them under the U.S. Constitution.
AZ.inPractice: State v. Superior Court (Ariz. 1984) approved checkpoints, and evidence from a lawful one is admissible (State v. Tykwinski, 1991). FindLaw (2025) reports they are held at least monthly.

AR.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Arkansas under both the state and U.S. constitutions, and police use them.
AR.inPractice: A checkpoint must follow a neutral, pre-set plan that limits officers' on-scene discretion (Whalen v. State, 2016), but no outside official has to approve it first (Sheridan v. State, 2007).
AR.detail: Must follow a neutral, pre-set plan

CA.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and common in California. The state Supreme Court approved them in Ingersoll v. Palmer (1987) if they follow neutral guidelines that limit officer discretion.
CA.inPractice: Advance publicity is a factor courts weigh but is not required (People v. Banks, 1993). FindLaw (2025) reports more than 2,500 checkpoints a year statewide.
CA.detail: Advance publicity helps but isn't required

CO.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Colorado and police use them. The Colorado Supreme Court reads the state constitution the same as the federal one on this issue.
CO.inPractice: People v. Rister and Orr v. People (Colo. 1990) upheld checkpoints. FindLaw (2025) reports they are held about once or twice a month under a state checkpoint manual.

CT.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Connecticut and police use them. The state Supreme Court upheld them under the Connecticut Constitution.
CT.inPractice: State v. Mikolinski, 775 A.2d 274 (Conn. 2001), is the leading ruling. FindLaw (2025) lists Connecticut among checkpoint states with no set frequency.

DE.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Delaware and used regularly. You can legally turn away before one if you obey traffic laws: a Delaware court held a legal U-turn before a checkpoint did not justify a stop.
DE.inPractice: The avoidance ruling is Howard v. Voshell (Del. Super. 1992), a trial-level decision. FindLaw (2025) reports checkpoints monthly early in the year and weekly from July to December.
DE.detail: Legal U-turn alone isn't grounds for a stop

DC.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Washington, D.C., and police use them. D.C.'s highest court has upheld them under the U.S. Constitution.
DC.inPractice: Galberth v. United States, 590 A.2d 990 (D.C. 1991), upheld checkpoint stops. FindLaw (2025) reports about one or two checkpoints a month in the District.

sources.label: IIHS, Summary of state court decisions on the constitutionality of sobriety checkpoints (Jan. 2020)
FindLaw, DUI Checkpoint Laws by State (updated Aug. 2025)

FL.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Florida and used often. They must follow written guidelines, set in advance, that control how officers choose which cars to stop.
FL.inPractice: State v. Jones (Fla. 1986) set the written-guidelines rule. In Campbell v. State (Fla. 1996), a checkpoint failed because its guidelines didn't say how vehicles would be selected.

GA.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and common in Georgia. Normal, legal driving that happens to avoid a checkpoint isn't grounds for a stop, but unusual evasive moves can give police reasonable suspicion.
GA.inPractice: LaFontaine v. State (Ga. 1998) requires, among other things, that a supervisor decide on the checkpoint in advance, not officers in the field. Taylor v. State (Ga. App. 2001) is the avoidance ruling.

HI.summary: Hawaii law lets county police run "intoxicant control roadblocks" with advance warning by signs or flares. Police can't stop you just for legally turning away before a checkpoint.
HI.inPractice: HRS 291E-20 requires stopping all cars or a set sequence and caps each roadblock at three hours in one spot. State v. Heapy (Haw. 2007) barred stops based only on a turn ahead of a checkpoint.

ID.summary: Sobriety checkpoints aren't allowed in Idaho. The Idaho Supreme Court held a DUI roadblock violated the state constitution without legislative authority, and state law allows roadblocks only to catch wanted suspects.
ID.inPractice: State v. Henderson (Idaho 1988) relied on art. I, sec. 17. Idaho Code 19-621 still limits roadblocks to apprehending people believed wanted for crimes, so DUI stops need individual suspicion.

IL.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and widely used in Illinois. The Illinois Supreme Court upheld them under the U.S. Constitution in People v. Bartley (1985).
IL.inPractice: Bartley approved a checkpoint run under preset procedures that limited officer discretion. FindLaw (2025) reports about one or two checkpoints a month per county.

IN.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Indiana and used occasionally. The Indiana Supreme Court said they don't automatically violate the state constitution, though a poorly run one can.
IN.inPractice: In State v. Gerschoffer (Ind. 2002) the court struck down the particular roadblock at issue. An appeals court has held that avoiding a checkpoint can justify a stop (Snyder v. State, 1989).
IN.detail: Avoiding a checkpoint can justify a stop

IA.summary: Iowa doesn't allow sobriety checkpoints. State law permits routine roadblocks only to check licenses, registration, safety equipment, and fish-and-game rules, so DUI checkpoints aren't authorized.
IA.inPractice: Iowa Code 321K.1 (2026) allows routine roadblocks "only as provided" there. Officers can still arrest impaired drivers found at a lawful license or equipment roadblock (State v. Day, 1995).

KS.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Kansas and used regularly. The Kansas Supreme Court upheld them and said no special authorization from the legislature is needed.
KS.inPractice: State v. Deskins (Kan. 1983) set factors for a reasonable checkpoint, and Davis v. Kansas Dept. of Revenue (1992) rejected the need for a statute. FindLaw (2025) reports one or two a month.

KY.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and common in Kentucky. Supervisors must set the time, place, and procedures in advance, and the checkpoint must be clearly visible to approaching drivers.
KY.inPractice: Commonwealth v. Buchanon (Ky. 2003) set these factors. Kentucky courts have held that turning to avoid a checkpoint can justify a stop (Bauder v. Commonwealth, Ky. 2009).
KY.detail: Avoiding a checkpoint can justify a stop

LA.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Louisiana. In 2000 the Louisiana Supreme Court reversed its earlier rulings and upheld them under the state constitution.
LA.inPractice: State v. Jackson (La. 2000) overruled State v. Church (1989). FindLaw (2025) says checkpoints are more common around holidays and major events.

FindLaw, DUI Checkpoint Laws by State (updated Aug. 2025)

ME.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Maine and used, especially in summer. The state must show a checkpoint was planned and run under guidelines that limit officer discretion.
ME.inPractice: State v. Kent (Me. 2011) put that burden on the state. Maine's high court has held that avoiding a checkpoint can be grounds for an investigative stop (State v. D'Angelo, 1992).
ME.detail: Avoiding a checkpoint can justify a stop

MD.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and used often in Maryland. The state's highest court upheld them under both the Maryland and U.S. constitutions.
MD.inPractice: Little v. State, 479 A.2d 903 (Md. 1984), is the leading ruling. FindLaw (2025) reports Maryland agencies hold checkpoints about weekly.

MA.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Massachusetts when run under written guidelines that leave officers little discretion. Checkpoints aimed at finding drugs are not allowed.
MA.inPractice: Commonwealth v. Shields (Mass. 1988) upheld them, and later cases threw out checkpoints that didn't follow guidelines. Further testing at a checkpoint needs reasonable suspicion (Commonwealth v. Murphy, 2009).

MI.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are banned in Michigan. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed Michigan's program in 1990, but the Michigan Supreme Court then held it violated the state constitution.
MI.inPractice: Sitz v. Department of State Police (Mich. 1993) rests on art. 1, sec. 11 of the Michigan Constitution. Police there need individual suspicion, such as a traffic violation, to stop a driver.

MN.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are banned in Minnesota. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that roadblocks stopping drivers without individual suspicion violate the state constitution.
MN.inPractice: Ascher v. Commissioner of Public Safety (Minn. 1994) relied on art. I, sec. 10; Gray v. Commissioner, decided the same day, applied it to a St. Paul checkpoint.

MS.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Mississippi and used often. Courts have upheld roadblocks that stop every vehicle, even without written procedures, because that removes officer discretion.
MS.inPractice: Miller v. State (Miss. 1979) and McLendon v. State (Miss. 2006) are the key rulings. FindLaw (2025) reports checkpoints about weekly.

MO.inPractice: State v. Canton (Mo. App. 1989) requires written procedures, and avoiding a checkpoint can justify a stop (Oughton v. Director of Revenue, 1996). How often local police still hold them is unconfirmed.

MT.inPractice: Those roadblocks (MCA 46-5-502, -510) need a written plan, supervisor approval, and 48-hour media notice. IIHS (2020) says checkpoints have run under this law; current DUI use is unconfirmed.

NE.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and used often in Nebraska. You can legally turn off before one as long as you follow traffic laws: avoiding a checkpoint does not, by itself, justify a stop.
NE.inPractice: Per IIHS's case-law summary, Nebraska courts have held avoidance alone doesn't justify a stop. State v. Piper (Neb. 2014) requires the checkpoint plan to be approved at the policymaking level.

NV.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and used often in Nevada. State law allows "administrative roadblocks" that are clearly visible and marked with a stop sign, a flashing red light, and advance "police stop" warnings.
NV.inPractice: NRS 484B.570 requires warning signs at least a quarter mile ahead in rural areas and 700 feet in urban areas. FindLaw (2025) reports checkpoints several times a month.

NH.inPractice: RSA 265:1-a sets the court-order rule. More than 60 New Hampshire agencies ran checkpoints on St. Patrick's Day 2026.

NJ.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in New Jersey and used several times a month. Courts have upheld them under the state and U.S. constitutions.
NJ.inPractice: In State v. Badessa (App. Div. 2004), stopping a driver for a lawful turn inside a checkpoint zone was invalid without posted no-turn warnings; the case was reversed on other grounds in 2005.

NM.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal and used often in New Mexico, especially in summer and on holidays. A legal turn away from a checkpoint, combined with other suspicious signs, can justify a stop.
NM.inPractice: City of Las Cruces v. Betancourt (N.M. App. 1987) is the leading checkpoint case; State v. Anaya (N.M. 2009) addressed turning away. Frequency is as reported by FindLaw (2025).

NY.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in New York and used often, especially on weekends and holidays. Courts have upheld them, and written guidelines aren't required.

NC.inPractice: G.S. 20-16.3A governs. The state Supreme Court has said officers may watch for drivers who turn away from a checkpoint and stop them to ask why (State v. Foreman, 2000).

ND.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in North Dakota under both the state and U.S. constitutions. Police don't have to give drivers a way to avoid a checkpoint.
ND.inPractice: City of Bismarck v. Uhden (N.D. 1994) upheld them; State v. Hahne (N.D. 2007) held no avoidance route is required. FindLaw (2025) says they're more common on holiday weekends.

OH.summary: Sobriety (OVI) checkpoints are legal in Ohio and police use them. Ohio appeals courts have upheld them under the state and U.S. constitutions.
OH.inPractice: State v. Bauer (Ohio App. 1994) and State v. Goines (Ohio App. 1984) are key rulings. FindLaw (2025) lists Ohio among checkpoint states with no set frequency.

OR.inPractice: Nelson v. Lane County and State v. Boyanovsky (Or. 1987) rest on art. I, sec. 9. The court said the legislature could authorize a program, but Oregon still doesn't use checkpoints (FindLaw, 2025).

SC.inPractice: IIHS (2020) notes South Carolina has no state checkpoint authority but conducts them. Unconfirmed: FindLaw (2025) says judicial approval is required, which no other source reviewed mentions.

SD.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in South Dakota and held about monthly. Avoiding a checkpoint isn't enough on its own for a stop, but other driving behavior seen before the stop can be.
SD.inPractice: State v. Rademaker (S.D. 2012) said avoidance alone isn't reasonable suspicion, but factors like time of night and wide turns can add up. Frequency is as reported by FindLaw (2025).

TN.summary: Sobriety checkpoints are legal in Tennessee if properly run. Supervisors, not officers at the scene, must decide where and how a checkpoint operates, and officer discretion must be limited.
TN.inPractice: State v. Downey (Tenn. 1997) and State v. Hicks (2001) set these rules. Avoiding a checkpoint may justify a stop, but a legal U-turn doesn't necessarily (State v. Binion, 1994).

TX.inPractice: Holt v. State (Tex. Crim. App. 1994) controls; bills to authorize checkpoints, such as 2009's SB 298, did not become law. Police rely on increased and saturation patrols instead.
